claim: Obesity has repeatedly been linked to reorganization of the gut microbiome.
source: Obesity has repeatedly been linked to reorganization of the gut microbiome, yet to this point obesity therapeutics have been targeted exclusively toward the human host.
evidence: This is a general statement about the established relationship between obesity and gut microbiome, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Obesity therapeutics have been targeted exclusively toward the human host.
source: Obesity has repeatedly been linked to reorganization of the gut microbiome, yet to this point obesity therapeutics have been targeted exclusively toward the human host.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of obesity drug development as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Gut microbe-targeted inhibition of the TMAO pathway protects mice against metabolic disturbances associated with diet-induced obesity.
source: Here, we show that gut microbe-targeted inhibition of the trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) pathway protects mice against the metabolic disturbances associated with diet-induced obesity (DIO) or leptin deficiency (Lepob/ob).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gut microbe-targeted inhibition of the TMAO pathway protects mice against metabolic disturbances associated with leptin deficiency.
source: Here, we show that gut microbe-targeted inhibition of the trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) pathway protects mice against the metabolic disturbances associated with diet-induced obesity (DIO) or leptin deficiency (Lepob/ob).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of gut microbial enzyme choline TMA-lyase (CutC) does not reduce food intake.
source: Small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial enzyme choline TMA-lyase (CutC) does not reduce food intake but is instead associated with alterations in the gut microbiome, improvement in glucose tolerance, and enhanced energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental measurements of food intake in treated mice.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of CutC is associated with alterations in the gut microbiome.
source: Small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial enzyme choline TMA-lyase (CutC) does not reduce food intake but is instead associated with alterations in the gut microbiome, improvement in glucose tolerance, and enhanced energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data of the gut microbiome.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of CutC is associated with improvement in glucose tolerance.
source: Small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial enzyme choline TMA-lyase (CutC) does not reduce food intake but is instead associated with alterations in the gut microbiome, improvement in glucose tolerance, and enhanced energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by glucose tolerance test data.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of CutC is associated with enhanced energy expenditure.
source: Small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial enzyme choline TMA-lyase (CutC) does not reduce food intake but is instead associated with alterations in the gut microbiome, improvement in glucose tolerance, and enhanced energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by indirect calorimetry measurements.

claim: Gut microbial CutC inhibition is associated with reorganization of host circadian control of phosphatidylcholine metabolism.
source: We also show that gut microbial CutC inhibition is associated with reorganization of host circadian control of both phosphatidylcholine and energy metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data collected at different circadian time points.

claim: Gut microbial CutC inhibition is associated with reorganization of host circadian control of energy metabolism.
source: We also show that gut microbial CutC inhibition is associated with reorganization of host circadian control of both phosphatidylcholine and energy metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by gene expression and metabolic measurements at different circadian time points.

claim: Gut microbe-derived trimethylamine (TMA) is a key regulator of the host circadian clock.
source: This study underscores the relationship between microbe and host metabolism and provides evidence that gut microbe-derived trimethylamine (TMA) is a key regulator of the host circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that inhibition of TMA production alters circadian gene expression and metabolic rhythms.

claim: Gut microbe-targeted enzyme inhibitors have potential as anti-obesity therapeutics.
source: This work also demonstrates that gut microbe-targeted enzyme inhibitors have potential as anti-obesity therapeutics.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that IMC treatment protects mice from obesity.

claim: The gut microbiome plays a central role in energy harvest from diet.
source: Our gut microbiome plays a central role in vital processes such as energy harvest from our diet, entraining our immune system during early life, xenobiotic metabolism, and the production of a diverse array of small molecule metabolites that are essential to human life (Brown and Hazen, 2015; Sonnenburg and Bäckhed, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The gut microbiome plays a central role in entraining the immune system during early life.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Obese mice harbor gut microbial communities with enhanced capacity to harvest energy from indigestible carbohydrates.
source: Specifically, obese mice harbor gut microbial communities with enhanced capacity to harvest energy from indigestible carbohydrates (Turnbaugh et al., 2006), and transplantation of either cecal contents or feces from either obese mice or humans is sufficient to promote obesity and related insulin resistance in germ-free mouse recipients (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ley et al., 2005; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Turnbaugh et al., 2006.

claim: Transplantation of cecal contents or feces from obese mice or humans is sufficient to promote obesity in germ-free mouse recipients.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Transplantation of cecal contents or feces from obese mice or humans is sufficient to promote insulin resistance in germ-free mouse recipients.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Antibiotic exposure in early life can predispose children to become overweight or obese later in life.
source: There is also accumulating evidence that antibiotic exposure in early life can predispose children to become overweight or obese later in life (Ajslev et al., 2011), and antibiotic treatment in mice prior to weaning increases obesity and related insulin resistance in adulthood (Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ajslev et al., 2011.

claim: Antibiotic treatment in mice prior to weaning increases obesity in adulthood.
source: There is also accumulating evidence that antibiotic exposure in early life can predispose children to become overweight or obese later in life (Ajslev et al., 2011), and antibiotic treatment in mice prior to weaning increases obesity and related insulin resistance in adulthood (Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: Small molecule inhibition of gut microbial choline to TMA transformation can significantly reduce atherosclerosis in mice.
source: We have recently shown that small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial transformation of choline into trimethylamine (TMA), the initial and rate-limiting step in trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) generation (Wang et al., 2011), can significantly reduce atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and adverse ventricular and kidney remodeling in mice (Roberts et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMAO can directly impact cell signaling in host platelets.
source: Although there is clear evidence that TMAO can directly impact cell signaling in host platelets and immune cells (Zhu et al., 2016; Seldin et al., 2016), it is still incompletely understood how the TMAO pathway is mechanistically linked to obesity-related cardiometabolic diseases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMAO can directly impact cell signaling in immune cells.
source: Although there is clear evidence that TMAO can directly impact cell signaling in host platelets and immune cells (Zhu et al., 2016; Seldin et al., 2016), it is still incompletely understood how the TMAO pathway is mechanistically linked to obesity-related cardiometabolic diseases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Manipulation of the gut microbiome can impact obesity in part via rewiring of the host circadian clock.
source: It is well appreciated that manipulation of the gut microbiome can impact obesity in part via rewiring of the host circadian clock, and reciprocally it has been shown that an intact circadian clock in the host can impact oscillatory behavior of gut microbiota (Org et al., 2015; Seldin et al., 2016; Thaiss et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An intact circadian clock in the host can impact oscillatory behavior of gut microbiota.
source: It is well appreciated that manipulation of the gut microbiome can impact obesity in part via rewiring of the host circadian clock, and reciprocally it has been shown that an intact circadian clock in the host can impact oscillatory behavior of gut microbiota (Org et al., 2015; Seldin et al., 2016; Thaiss et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IMC effectively reduces levels of both TMA and TMAO when administered in a high fat diet.
source: When administered in an HFD, IMC effectively reduces levels of both the primary product of CutC TMA and the host liver-derived co-metabolite TMAO (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: IMC was effective in blunting diet-induced obesity.
source: IMC was effective in blunting diet-induced obesity (DIO) (Figure 1c), without altering food intake (Figure 1d).
evidence: This statement is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: IMC did not alter food intake in diet-induced obesity mice.
source: IMC was effective in blunting diet-induced obesity (DIO) (Figure 1c), without altering food intake (Figure 1d).
evidence: This statement is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: DIO mice treated with IMC showed improvements in glucose tolerance.
source: DIO mice treated with IMC also showed improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 1e), exhibited marked reductions in plasma insulin levels in fed mice but not under fasting conditions (Figure 1f) and had significant reductions in fat mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: DIO mice treated with IMC exhibited marked reductions in plasma insulin levels in fed mice.
source: DIO mice treated with IMC also showed improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 1e), exhibited marked reductions in plasma insulin levels in fed mice but not under fasting conditions (Figure 1f) and had significant reductions in fat mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma insulin data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: DIO mice treated with IMC did not show reductions in plasma insulin levels under fasting conditions.
source: DIO mice treated with IMC also showed improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 1e), exhibited marked reductions in plasma insulin levels in fed mice but not under fasting conditions (Figure 1f) and had significant reductions in fat mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma insulin data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: DIO mice treated with IMC had significant reductions in fat mass.
source: DIO mice treated with IMC also showed improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 1e), exhibited marked reductions in plasma insulin levels in fed mice but not under fasting conditions (Figure 1f) and had significant reductions in fat mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: The ability of IMC to reduce adiposity was specific to high fat feeding and was not seen in low fat-fed mice.
source: It is important to note that the ability of IMC to reduce adiposity was specific to high fat feeding and was not seen in low fat-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by body composition data comparing high fat and low fat diets shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: IMC treatment did not significantly alter intestinal fatty acid absorption.
source: Also, IMC treatment did not significantly alter intestinal fatty acid absorption or hepatic steatosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,f and 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by fatty acid absorption data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: IMC treatment did not significantly alter hepatic steatosis.
source: Also, IMC treatment did not significantly alter intestinal fatty acid absorption or hepatic steatosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,f and 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by hepatic lipid data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,f.

claim: IMC effectively lowered both TMA and TMAO levels in Lepob/ob mice.
source: As expected, IMC effectively lowered both TMA and TMAO levels in Lepob/ob mice (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma TMA and TMAO measurements shown in Figure 1g and h.

claim: IMC dramatically protected Lepob/ob mice from body weight gain.
source: Quite unexpectedly, IMC dramatically protected Lepob/ob mice from body weight gain, where some of the drug-treated mice were 15–20 g lighter than control Lepob/ob mice (Figure 1i).
evidence: This statement is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: IMC-driven protection from obesity in Lepob/ob mice was not associated with decreased food intake.
source: Notably, IMC-driven protection from obesity was not associated with decreased food intake, which was paradoxically higher overall in IMC-treated mice (Figure 1j).
evidence: This statement is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Food intake was paradoxically higher overall in IMC-treated Lepob/ob mice.
source: Notably, IMC-driven protection from obesity was not associated with decreased food intake, which was paradoxically higher overall in IMC-treated mice (Figure 1j).
evidence: This statement is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: IMC treatment promoted large increases in energy expenditure through both the light and dark cycles in Lepob/ob mice.
source: Instead, IMC treatment promoted large increases in energy expenditure through both the light and dark cycles (Figure 1l, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-c)
evidence: This statement is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 1l and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-c.

claim: IMC effectively reduced body weight and adiposity in Lepob/ob mice, but this was not associated with improvements in glucose tolerance.
source: Although IMC effectively reduced body weight and adiposity in Lepob/ob mice, this was not associated with improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 1k).
evidence: This statement is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1k.

claim: IMC did not promote weight loss in mice with established obesity, but it did effectively reduce the trajectory of weight gain.
source: Although IMC did not promote weight loss, it did effectively reduce the trajectory of weight gain and improved glucose tolerance in this obesity treatment model (Figure 1—figure supplement 4d, f).
evidence: This statement is supported by body weight data in the obesity treatment model shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4d.

claim: IMC improved glucose tolerance in mice with established obesity.
source: Although IMC did not promote weight loss, it did effectively reduce the trajectory of weight gain and improved glucose tolerance in this obesity treatment model (Figure 1—figure supplement 4d, f).
evidence: This statement is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4f.

claim: During the early phases of the obesity treatment study, IMC-treated mice exhibited unexpected increased food intake compared to controls.
source: During the early phases of this obesity treatment study, IMC-treated mice again exhibited unexpected increased food intake compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e).
evidence: This statement is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4e.

claim: Long-term IMC treatment did not promote liver toxicity.
source: It is important to note that long-term IMC treatment did not promote either liver or renal toxicity, as shown by normal plasma enzyme levels as well as normal tissue histology in liver and adipose depots (Figure 1—figure supplement 5a-e).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma enzyme levels and histology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5a-e.

claim: Long-term IMC treatment did not promote renal toxicity.
source: It is important to note that long-term IMC treatment did not promote either liver or renal toxicity, as shown by normal plasma enzyme levels as well as normal tissue histology in liver and adipose depots (Figure 1—figure supplement 5a-e).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma enzyme levels and histology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5a-e.

claim: Principal coordinate analysis of RNA expression profiles showed clear separation of adipose gene expression between HFD control vs. HFD with IMC.
source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCA) of RNA expression profiles showed clear separation of adipose gene expression between HFD control vs. HFD with IMC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4g).
evidence: This statement is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4g.

claim: The most differentially expressed genes altered by IMC were enriched in common pathways of adipogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, inflammation, and cytokine signaling.
source: The most differentially expressed genes altered by IMC were enriched in common pathways of adipogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, inflammation, and cytokine signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 4i).
evidence: This statement is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4i.

claim: IMC treatment in HFD-fed mice resulted in significant restructuring of the cecal microbiome at every taxonomic level.
source: IMC treatment in HFD-fed mice resulted in significant restructuring of the cecal microbiome at every taxonomic level (Figure 2a–e).
evidence: This statement is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2a-e.

claim: PCA of microbial taxa revealed distinct clusters, indicating that IMC promoted restructuring of the cecal microbiome.
source: PCA of microbial taxa revealed distinct clusters, indicating that IMC promoted restructuring of the cecal microbiome (Figure 2a).
evidence: This statement is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: HFD-fed IMC-treated mice had large increases in Verrucomicrobia and Bacteroidetes at the phylum level.
source: At the phylum level, HFD-fed IMC-treated mice had large increases in Verrucomicrobia and Bacteroidetes, and significant reductions in Firmicutes (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome composition data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: HFD-fed IMC-treated mice had significant reductions in Firmicutes at the phylum level.
source: At the phylum level, HFD-fed IMC-treated mice had large increases in Verrucomicrobia and Bacteroidetes, and significant reductions in Firmicutes (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome composition data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes has been correlated with obesity in both humans and mice.
source: Of note, the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, which has been correlated with obesity in both humans and mice (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ley et al., 2005; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009), is significantly reduced by IMC treatment of the HFD-fed mice (Figure 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes is significantly reduced by IMC treatment of HFD-fed mice.
source: Of note, the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, which has been correlated with obesity in both humans and mice (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ley et al., 2005; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009), is significantly reduced by IMC treatment of the HFD-fed mice (Figure 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome composition data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: IMC promoted significant reductions in the proportions of Desulfovibrionaceae, Butyrovibrio, Bilophia, Peptococcaceae, and Dorea.
source: Performance of linear discriminant analysis coupled with effect size measurements (LEfSe analysis) revealed that IMC promoted significant reductions in the proportions of the taxa Desulfovibrionaceae, Butyrovibrio, Bilophia, Peptococcaceae, and Dorea, and increases in Odoribacter, Roseburia, and several members of the Clostridiaceae family (Figure 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: IMC promoted increases in Odoribacter, Roseburia, and several members of the Clostridiaceae family.
source: Performance of linear discriminant analysis coupled with effect size measurements (LEfSe analysis) revealed that IMC promoted significant reductions in the proportions of the taxa Desulfovibrionaceae, Butyrovibrio, Bilophia, Peptococcaceae, and Dorea, and increases in Odoribacter, Roseburia, and several members of the Clostridiaceae family (Figure 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Increases in Akkermansia were significantly correlated with plasma TMA level in DIO mice.
source: We also examined whether the proportions of cecal genera were significantly correlated with plasma TMA, body weight, and glucose tolerance in DIO mice, and found that increases in Akkermansia and reductions in Bilophila were significantly correlated with plasma TMA level, and similar yet non-significant trends were found with body weight and glucose tolerance (Figure 2e).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Reductions in Bilophila were significantly correlated with plasma TMA level in DIO mice.
source: We also examined whether the proportions of cecal genera were significantly correlated with plasma TMA, body weight, and glucose tolerance in DIO mice, and found that increases in Akkermansia and reductions in Bilophila were significantly correlated with plasma TMA level, and similar yet non-significant trends were found with body weight and glucose tolerance (Figure 2e).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: IMC rapidly reorganized the gut microbiome within 48 hr of the first drug exposure.
source: Remarkably, IMC rapidly reorganized the gut microbiome within 48 hr of the first drug exposure, and similar changes were seen after 6 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b) and a chronic treatment of 20 weeks (Figure 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: IMC significantly altered the cecal microbiome in Lepob/ob mice.
source: Similar to HFD-fed mice (Figure 2a–e), IMC also significantly altered the cecal microbiome in Lepob/ob mice (Figure 2f-i).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2f-i.

claim: In Lepob/ob mice, IMC significantly reduced the proportions of Adlercreutzia, Rikenellaceae, Peptococcaceae, and Clostridiales.
source: In Lepob/ob mice, IMC significantly reduced the proportions of Adlercreutzia, Rikenellaceae, Peptococcaceae, and Clostridiales, while increasing levels of Molicutes, Allobaculum, Peptostreptococcaceae, and Akkermansia (Figure 2g–h).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2g-h.

claim: In Lepob/ob mice, IMC increased levels of Molicutes, Allobaculum, Peptostreptococcaceae, and Akkermansia.
source: In Lepob/ob mice, IMC significantly reduced the proportions of Adlercreutzia, Rikenellaceae, Peptococcaceae, and Clostridiales, while increasing levels of Molicutes, Allobaculum, Peptostreptococcaceae, and Akkermansia (Figure 2g–h).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2g-h.

claim: In Lepob/ob mice, IMC-induced alterations in Akkermansia, Clostridiales, and Allobaculum were significantly associated with circulating TMA and body weight.
source: Correlation analysis in Lepob/ob mice revealed that IMC-induced alterations in Akkermansia, Clostridiales, and Allobaculum were significantly associated with circulating TMA and body weight (Figure 2i).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Akkermansia muciniphila has been pursued as a therapeutic probiotic species for diabetes amelioration in other studies.
source: Notably, in both the Lepob/ob and DIO models, the large increase in the proportions of Verrucomicrobia phylum seen with IMC are largely explained by increased level of Akkermansia muciniphila, which has been pursued as a therapeutic probiotic species for diabetes amelioration in other studies (Everard et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2014; Org et al., 2015) and is correlated to TMA and body weight phenotypes in the current study.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Plasma levels of choline, carnitine, and TMA were relatively low during the light cycle, and peak at the beginning of the dark cycle when mice are most active and consuming food.
source: Plasma levels of both choline, carnitine, and TMA were relatively low during the light cycle, and peak at the beginning of the dark cycle when mice are most active and consuming food (Figure 3a).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: TMAO showed more modest oscillatory behavior compared to choline, carnitine, and TMA.
source: However, TMAO showed more modest oscillatory behavior (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma TMAO measurements shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,d.

claim: Hepatic expression of Fmo3 is quite low during the day but increases 6-fold during the early dark cycle.
source: We also found that the hepatic expression of flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (Fmo3) is quite low during the day but increases 6-fold during the early dark cycle (Figure 3a).

claim: The pattern for Fmo3 expression is opposite in WAT compared to liver.

claim: Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in skeletal muscle.
source: It is important to note that Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in skeletal (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) and cardiac muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and shows no oscillatory behavior in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), where it is important for sensing the 'fishy odor' smell of TMA (Thaiss et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in cardiac muscle.
source: It is important to note that Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in skeletal (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) and cardiac muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and shows no oscillatory behavior in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), where it is important for sensing the 'fishy odor' smell of TMA (Thaiss et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Taar5 shows no oscillatory behavior in the olfactory bulb.
source: It is important to note that Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in skeletal (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) and cardiac muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and shows no oscillatory behavior in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), where it is important for sensing the 'fishy odor' smell of TMA (Thaiss et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Taar5 is important for sensing the 'fishy odor' smell of TMA in the olfactory bulb.
source: It is important to note that Taar5 oscillation specifically occurs in skeletal (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) and cardiac muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and shows no oscillatory behavior in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), where it is important for sensing the 'fishy odor' smell of TMA (Thaiss et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IMC treatment effectively lowered circulating TMA and TMAO at every time point.
source: In this circadian study, IMC treatment effectively lowered circulating TMA and TMAO at every time point, yet there were still highly rhythmic low levels of plasma TMA and TMAO observed, possibly originating from microbial metabolism of non-choline (i.e., carnitine, γ-butyrobetaine, betaine, trimethyllysine) nutrient sources via microbial enzymes that are not inhibited by IMC (Li et al., 2013; Wallrabenstein et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, d).
evidence: This statement is supported by plasma metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, d.

claim: In the liver, microbial choline TMA lyase inhibition modestly increased the peak amplitude of Bmal1 and Nr1d1.
source: In the liver, microbial choline TMA lyase inhibition modestly increased the peak amplitude of the core clock transcription factors Bmal1 and Nr1d1 yet blunted the rhythmic expression of Cry1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In the liver, microbial choline TMA lyase inhibition blunted the rhythmic expression of Cry1.
source: In the liver, microbial choline TMA lyase inhibition modestly increased the peak amplitude of the core clock transcription factors Bmal1 and Nr1d1 yet blunted the rhythmic expression of Cry1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In WAT, choline TMA lyase inhibition blunted the peak amplitude of Bmal1.
source: In WAT, choline TMA lyase inhibition blunted the peak amplitude of Bmal1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In skeletal muscle, IMC-treated mice showed marked increases at all time points for Nr1d1.
source: However, in skeletal muscle, we found the most striking differences in the core clock machinery where IMC-treated mice showed marked increases at all time points for Nr1d1 and a near-complete phase shift for Cry1 (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: In skeletal muscle, IMC-treated mice showed a near-complete phase shift for Cry1.
source: However, in skeletal muscle, we found the most striking differences in the core clock machinery where IMC-treated mice showed marked increases at all time points for Nr1d1 and a near-complete phase shift for Cry1 (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: IMC is poorly absorbed in the host and selectively accumulates in gut microbiota.
source: Prior studies have confirmed that IMC is poorly absorbed in the host and selectively accumulates in gut microbiota (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IMC does not alter the expression of core clock genes in the olfactory bulb where Taar5 is abundantly expressed throughout the day and does not oscillate diurnally.
source: Critically, IMC does not alter the expression of core clock genes in areas of the central nervous system like the olfactory bulb where Taar5 is abundantly expressed throughout the day and does not oscillate diurnally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Taar5 does not oscillate in the olfactory bulb and the hypothesis that IMC effects are mediated through TMA-Taar5 signaling.

claim: In mice fed a HFD to induce obesity, IMC treatment significantly altered the oscillatory patterns of key host metabolic hormones insulin, leptin, and adiponectin.
source: Also, in mice fed a HFD to induce obesity, we found that IMC treatment significantly altered the oscillatory patterns of key host metabolic hormones insulin, leptin, and adiponectin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-c), which is likely to play a modulatory role in downstream lipid metabolic phenotypes.
evidence: This statement is supported by hormone measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-c.

claim: In HFD-fed mice, IMC treatment altered the circadian oscillation in gene expression for Cry1 and Per2.
source: Furthermore, in HFD-fed mice IMC treatment altered the circadian oscillation in gene expression for cryptochrome 1 (Cry1) and period 2 (Per2) and key genes involved in lipid metabolism including carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1α (Cpt1α) and betaine homocysteine methyltransferase (Bhmt) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d-i).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d-i.

claim: In HFD-fed mice, IMC treatment altered the circadian oscillation in gene expression for Cpt1α and Bhmt.
source: Furthermore, in HFD-fed mice IMC treatment altered the circadian oscillation in gene expression for cryptochrome 1 (Cry1) and period 2 (Per2) and key genes involved in lipid metabolism including carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1α (Cpt1α) and betaine homocysteine methyltransferase (Bhmt) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d-i).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d-i.

claim: The composition of the gut microbiome is under circadian regulation.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bacterial communities oscillate in a highly circadian manner at the phylum level.
source: These reports show that even at the phylum level, bacterial communities oscillate in a highly circadian manner, and gut microbe community oscillation can impact host metabolic rhythms that are linked to human disease (Org et al., 2015; Seldin et al., 2016; Thaiss et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gut microbe community oscillation can impact host metabolic rhythms that are linked to human disease.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microbial production of TMA has striking effects on circadian oscillations in gut microbial communities.

evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-c.

claim: PCA revealed distinct group clusters, indicating that IMC promoted restructuring of the cecal microbial community composition in a circadian manner.
source: PCA revealed distinct group clusters, indicating that IMC promoted restructuring of the cecal microbial community composition in a circadian manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: At the phylum level, IMC treatment results in large relative increases in Bacteroidetes, while lowering the overall levels of Firmicutes at all time points.
source: At the phylum level, IMC treatment results in large relative increases in Bacteroidetes, while lowering the overall levels of Firmicutes at all time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome composition data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: IMC treatment promoted a significant increase in the abundance of A. muciniphila.
source: Interestingly, IMC treatment promoted a significant increase in the abundance of A. muciniphila, proportions of which have been reported to be inversely correlated with body weight and insulin sensitivity in numerous studies in both rodents and humans (Everard et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2014; Org et al., 2015; Figure 2b, d, g and h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in multiple figures.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IMC treatment increased the level of S24-7 Bacteroidetes family members.
source: In addition, IMC treatment increased the level of S24-7 Bacteroidetes family members, which have recently been reported to be depleted in several mouse models of obesity-related metabolic disturbance (Koeth et al., 2014; Li et al., 2018; Lieber et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: S24-7 Bacteroidetes family members have recently been reported to be depleted in several mouse models of obesity-related metabolic disturbance.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The most significant alterations in the plasma metabolome by IMC were seen during the ZT10 to ZT14 transition.
source: SPICA was utilized based on its unique ability to highlight subtle changes in the metabolome via analysis of metabolite pairs, which vastly reduces normalization issues endemic to mass spectrometry derived small molecule datasets (i.e., untargeted metabolomics). This approach delivers a more comprehensive picture of the overall metabolomic signature in TMA-regulated host circadian clock compared to the traditional single-metabolite oriented metabolomic data tools. Although there were clear IMC-induced metabolomic alterations at every time point, the most significant alterations were seen during the ZT10 to ZT14 transition, which coincides with the light to dark transition when mice typically begin to forage for food.
evidence: This statement is supported by SPICA analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: Choline TMA lyase inhibition was associated with alterations in diurnal rhythms of phosphatidylcholine (PC) co-metabolites.
source: In particular, we found that choline TMA lyase inhibition was associated with alterations in diurnal rhythms of phosphatidylcholine (PC) co-metabolites (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statement is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Gut microbial TMA lyase inhibition caused near-complete circadian phase shifts for two PC species (16:0/22:6 and 18:1/18:1).
source: Gut microbial TMA lyase inhibition caused near-complete circadian phase shifts for two PC species (16:0/22:6 and 18:1/18:1), and two saturated species (16:0 and 18:0) of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), which showed robust oscillatory behavior distinct from control mice (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statement is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Two saturated species (16:0 and 18:0) of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) showed robust oscillatory behavior distinct from control mice.
source: Gut microbial TMA lyase inhibition caused near-complete circadian phase shifts for two PC species (16:0/22:6 and 18:1/18:1), and two saturated species (16:0 and 18:0) of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), which showed robust oscillatory behavior distinct from control mice (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statement is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The oscillatory behavior of genes involved in PC synthesis including CKα and PEMT were significantly altered in TMA lyase inhibited mice.
source: Furthermore, we found that the oscillatory behavior of genes involved in PC synthesis including choline kinase α (CKα) and phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase (PEMT) were significantly altered in TMA lyase inhibited mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, d).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, d.

claim: IMC did not alter key plasma hormones (corticosterone or insulin) or lipids (non-esterified fatty acids) that are known to have strong effects on phospholipid metabolism.
source: It is important to note that IMC did not alter key plasma hormones (corticosterone or insulin) or lipids (non-esterified fatty acids) that are known to have strong effects on phospholipid metabolism themselves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This statement is supported by hormone and lipid measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Gut microbial TMA production from the choline TMA lyase CutC is a critical determinant of host circadian rhythms in PC homeostasis.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that gut microbial TMA production from the choline TMA lyase CutC is a critical determinant of host circadian rhythms in PC homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolomics and gene expression data showing that IMC alters circadian rhythms in PC species and PC synthesis genes.

claim: Gut microbial communities display circadian changes.

claim: Microbes transplanted from mice receiving choline TMA lyase inhibitors results in significant taxonomic differences from mice receiving control microbiota.
source: Gut microbial communities display circadian changes and microbes transplanted from mice receiving choline TMA lyase inhibitors results in significant taxonomic differences from mice receiving control microbiota (Figure 5b–d).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 5b-d.

claim: The gut microbial community from HFD + IMC mice conferred reduced visceral adiposity to donor mice challenged with 8 weeks of HFD.
source: Interestingly, the gut microbial community from HFD + IMC mice conferred reduced visceral adiposity to donor mice challenged with 8 weeks of HFD and these effects are independent of body weight, liver weight, and TMA/TMAO production (Figure 5e–i).
evidence: This statement is supported by gnotobiotic mouse data shown in Figure 5e-i.

claim: The effects of HFD + IMC microbiota on reduced visceral adiposity are independent of body weight, liver weight, and TMA/TMAO production.
source: Interestingly, the gut microbial community from HFD + IMC mice conferred reduced visceral adiposity to donor mice challenged with 8 weeks of HFD and these effects are independent of body weight, liver weight, and TMA/TMAO production (Figure 5e–i).

claim: The transplanted cecal microbiota from HFD + IMC mice altered gene expression in a tissue-specific manner.
source: Additionally, the transplanted cecal microbiota from HFD + IMC mice altered gene expression in a tissue-specific manner in alignment with our other studies (Figure 3b).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data in gnotobiotic mice.

claim: The expression of multiple circadian genes in the skeletal muscle, including Nr1d1, Cry1, Cry2, and Per2, was significantly reduced by the HFD + IMC microbiota at ZT14.
source: Specifically, the expression of multiple circadian genes in the skeletal muscle, including Nr1d1, Cry1, Cry2, and Per2, was significantly reduced by the HFD + IMC microbiota at ZT14, the same time point that was highlighted in our unbiased metabolomics analysis (Figure 5j, Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5j.

claim: In WAT, Foxo1 expression was significantly increased at ZT14 vs. ZT2 only in mice that received an HFD cecal microbiota.
source: In WAT, Foxo1 expression was significantly increased at ZT14 vs. ZT2 only in mice that received an HFD cecal microbiota and in contrast Adrb1 was increased at ZT14 in mice colonized with an HFD + IMC microbiota, but not those with the HFD gut microbes (Figure 5k).
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5k.

claim: Adrb1 was increased at ZT14 in mice colonized with an HFD + IMC microbiota, but not those with the HFD gut microbes.

evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5k.

claim: Circulating TMAO levels are dose-dependently associated with obesity in humans.
source: Interestingly, recent meta-analysis of clinical studies demonstrated that circulating TMAO levels are dose-dependently associated with obesity in humans (Moreira Júnior et al., 2019), highlighting the potential translation of this work.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis study.

claim: IMC lowers the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, which is known to be elevated in obese humans and rodents.
source: For instance, IMC lowers the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes (Figures 2c, 5b and c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), which is known to be elevated in obese humans and rodents (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Ley et al., 2005; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by microbiome data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have shown favorable effects of A. muciniphila in obesity and diabetes.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Supplementation with A. muciniphila can improve glucose tolerance in obese mice.
source: Supplementation with A. muciniphila can improve glucose tolerance in obese mice (Everard et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2014; Org et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increases in A. muciniphila are consistently seen in mice treated with TMA lyase inhibitor.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Nearly a quarter of commonly used host-targeted drugs have microbiome-altering properties.

claim: TMAO binding to PERK regulates the expression of the forkhead transcription factor Foxo1.

claim: PERK was recently shown to regulate circadian rhythms that support sleep/wake patterns and cancer growth.
